content.text: Whether a value sits on the stack or the heap is an implementation detail that depends on context and changes between JIT releases. What really separates value types from reference types is what a variable holds: a struct variable holds the data itself, so every assignment copies it. Choose
by that behavior, not by where you think the memory goes.

The belief goes like this: value types (

, your structs) live on the stack, reference types (classes, arrays, strings) live on the heap, and that's what makes them different. It's in countless tutorials and interview answers, and Microsoft's own docs described value types that way for years.
It survives because it's half true. A local

in an ordinary method really does live in the method's stack frame, or in a CPU register, and vanishes when the method returns. Boxing is usually drawn as a value being copied from the stack to the heap, which reinforces the picture. And developers coming from C++ are used to choosing stack or heap themselves.

The trouble is that the rule turns one case of an implementation detail into a definition. It's wrong for fields, array elements, captured variables and async methods, and it hides what actually changes your program's behavior: copying.
The real difference: what a variable holds

contains the instance itself. A variable of a reference type contains a reference to an instance stored elsewhere. Assignment, passing an argument and returning a result all copy what the variable holds. For a reference type that's the reference, so two variables can point at one object and see each other's changes. For a value type it's the whole value, so every variable has its own independent copy.

That's the contract the language guarantees, and the part you observe in code. One detail catches people out: copying a struct copies its fields, and a reference-type field is copied as a reference. If your struct holds a

Reference types don't always live on the heap either
The mirror-image rule is breaking down too. The JIT uses

to find objects that can't outlive the method that creates them, and can allocate those on the stack: boxes since .NET 9, plus small fixed-size arrays and delegates in .NET 10. None of this changes what your code means, only where the bytes go, which is exactly why "stack or heap?" is the wrong question to design around.

content.text: How to apply it in your project
Is the type a value, like an amount, a coordinate or a date range, or a thing with an identity that changes over time, like an order? Things with identity should be classes.
Microsoft's design guidelines suggest a struct only for a single, immutable value under 16 bytes that won't be boxed often. Mark it
so the compiler enforces the immutability.
Look for code that reads a struct from a list, dictionary or array, changes it, and never writes it back. In hot paths, also look for structs passed as
or as an interface: each one is a box.

items.title: Measure before you claim a win

content.text: Prove performance changes with a benchmark that reports allocations, such as BenchmarkDotNet's
. The JIT may already remove the allocation you want to save, or your change may add boxes elsewhere.

items.text: Value versus reference is about what a variable holds and what gets copied, not where memory is allocated.
A struct lives wherever its variable lives, which often means inside a heap object, array, closure or state machine.
The JIT is free to move things: in .NET 10 it can stack-allocate some non-escaping objects and keep struct fields in registers.
